items.title: Ramsey Lewis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: First of all, I don’t know Barack Obama – President Barack Obama – personally. I know him, but I don’t know him personally.

ctx.x: When we see now that we have somebody that you know personally, how does this impact your views, your perspective on the leadership and the direction of this country?

First of all, I don’t know Barack Obama – President Barack Obama – personally. I know him, but I don’t know him personally. But I know enough about him to know that he expected more cooperation. He went into this thing thinking about everybody just waiting an opportunity for a guy to say, “Let’s make this country better.” He was thinking that if not a majority of politicians, surely the country would rise up and say, “How do we make the country better? Show us the way. We’ll pressure the politicians who are…

Okay. The game of politics. That’s the way it’s played. We got to get our boy in. I don’t care if he’s black, purple, green. We got to get our boy in. Just what happens if you’re black? Does that have anything to do with it? Oh no, oh no. But we got to get our boy in. Where are the American citizens? If all these people saying these terrible things that are tearing our country down, then surely there would be – say a million of them are saying. There’s 299 million – let’s take the kids away – there’s 200 million…

items.title: Ramsey Lewis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I would love to return to this. Here we are, sitting in Chicago. We have a black President from Chicago.

ctx.x: God help me to be a better person. I think in their own way they’re sincere. I think so. But Monday is business as usual. “No, we can’t allow them” – they – they, them, they, them. What happened to us? Us, as in humanity? Is it religion, is it spirituality that can help us gain this oneness? Because it’s not until – we speak of the deficit. We speak of all the problems of our country growing, on one hand, how we’re being surpassed by other countries in certain areas – but it’s not until we come together as…

I would love to return to this. Here we are, sitting in Chicago. We have a black President from Chicago. We’re going to return to this, the political dialogue, but I wanted to go back. Let me just use this as a segue. Instead of “My country tis of thee,” how about “Our country tis of thee”?

items.title: Ramsey Lewis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: There’s a picture of you with him.

ctx.x: I’m through. I think you know where I was going with that. It angers me, though.

And rightly so, because you’ve seen seven-plus decades of the evolution of this country. Over – when I look over on this other wall around the corner, there’s a picture of you with another Chicagoan in the White House, who is the first one to be in that White House to come from the African-American community in Chicago, yet alone any African-American community in this country. There’s a picture of you with him. When we talk about leadership and we talk about this country . . .
